body_markdown:
Switching to a new nonprofit CRM is a chance to reset how your organization works, cares for supporters, and grows. But, according to research,


[55% of CRM migration projects fail](https://syncmatters.com/blog/10-proven-crm-migration-best-practices) —not because the technology breaks, but because the planning behind it was thin.


That gap between promise and outcome almost always comes down to the same handful of mistakes. Here’s where migrations most often go wrong, and how to make sure yours doesn’t.


## The Top Four Common CRM Migration Pitfalls


Most failed CRM migrations trace back to one of four patterns. Here’s what each looks like, and what to do instead.


### 1. Rushing Without a Clear Strategy


Many nonprofits hurry into a new system before a big appeal or gala. The intent is well-meaning, but without a clear strategy, the new CRM quickly starts to feel like the old one with a different logo.


Watch for these signs you’re moving too fast:


- **No defined success metrics:** You can’t say what growth should look like after migration, whether that’s higher donor retention, more recurring gifts, or faster board reporting.


- **No process mapping:** Data moves without anyone asking how work actually flows, so gaps and double work carry straight into the new system.


- **Unrealistic timelines:** The team is trying to finish a full migration right before GivingTuesday or a major event, leaving no room to catch mistakes.


The fix for all three starts with slowing down:


- **Define success:** Decide what success actually looks like before you move a single record. That might be cutting reconciliation time in half, hitting a specific recurring-gift growth rate, or getting board reports out same-day instead of a week later.


- **Map processes:** Consider how donor intake, event registration, volunteer onboarding, and campaigns actually work today and how you want them to work going forward.


- **Plan accordingly:** Schedule 6 to 8 weeks of prep before you move a single record, with dedicated time for testing and training built into the schedule.


### 2. Underestimating Data Cleanup and Mapping


The new CRM only works as well as the data you put into it. Skip the cleanup step, and problems like duplicate donor records just move with you into the new system.


Here are some common issues worth catching before migration:


- Duplicate donor records with slightly different names


- Outdated addresses, emails, and phone numbers


- Inconsistent gift codes and campaign names


- Confusion between household and individual supporter records


**From the field:**[Habitat for Humanity of Springfield, Missouri](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/habitat-springfield-gala-case-study-185k-tailgate-theme/) went into its CRM transition with a new team and messy historical data, on top of a long-running gala event that needed a full refresh. Untangling that data before migration, rather than during it, was part of what let the team raise $185,000 against a $135,000 goal.


### 3. Leaving Staff Out of the Process


The staff running fundraising, events, and volunteer programs every day know exactly where the current system breaks down, and leaving them out of the decision just guarantees those same breakdowns show up again in the new one.


A cross-functional migration team helps close that gap. At minimum, include power users from fundraising, marketing, volunteer management, events, and finance. They’ll flag missing fields, awkward workflows, and reporting needs long before go-live.


**From the field:** When


[Jewish Family Services of Washtenaw County](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/jewish-family-services-data-migration-and-onboarding-case-study/) onboarded to Giveffect, staff across the organization, not just IT, went through five structured training sessions together. That involvement meant the whole team was actively using the system, from account setup to thank-you notes, within days of go-live.


### 4. Rebuilding Old Manual Habits Instead of Automating


The whole point of consolidating is to stop doing things by hand. But old habits are sticky, and it’s easy to migrate systems without migrating the way your team actually works.


Here’s what these


[workarounds](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/nonprofit-crm-workarounds/) often look like in practice:


- Manually sending welcome emails instead of triggering a welcome series


- Hand-tracking lapsed donors instead of flagging them automatically


- Copying and pasting volunteer confirmations between tools


- Piecing together event follow-up from separate lists


This is the moment to set up high-impact automated workflows instead:


- A welcome series for new donors


- Thank-you messages for recurring gifts


- Event follow-up and survey emails


- Volunteer re-engagement messages


It’s also the moment to connect the systems that still sit outside the CRM. If online giving forms, peer-to-peer pages, and volunteer sign-ups aren’t integrated from day one, staff will keep exporting and importing data between tools no matter how good the core platform is.


**From the field:**[UCLA UniCamp](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/ucla-unicamp-boosting-fundraising-efficiency-by-150-more-per-student-with-giveffect/) used to burn hours manually importing and exporting donation, event, and volunteer data across systems. After automating that work with Giveffect, the team raised nearly the same total with 130 fewer volunteers, about $150 more per student, freeing up time to focus on the mission instead of data entry.


## How to Plan Your Next Migration


With year-end fundraising approaching, late summer is the moment to decide honestly whether you can complete a thoughtful migration now, or whether an early-year move deserves more runway.


No matter the time,


[preparing your organization for a major CRM transition](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/how-to-prepare-for-a-nonprofit-crm-transition/) requires you to work through a few questions:


- What does success look like in six months, and how will you measure it?


- How much of your current data actually needs cleaning before it moves?


- Who needs a seat at the table, and who owns the system after go-live?


- Which manual workarounds should this migration eliminate, not just relocate?

## FAQs


**How long does a nonprofit CRM migration typically take?**


8 to 12 weeks, from data cleanup through go-live. Larger data volumes and more legacy systems push you toward the longer end.


**What’s the biggest reason CRM migrations fail?**


People, not technology: unclear ownership, weak training, or staff left out of planning.


**Should we migrate before or after a major fundraising event?**


Before, with several months of runway if possible. Migrating right before GivingTuesday or a gala leaves no room for testing or training to absorb mistakes. Late summer, ahead of fall appeals, is the safer window.


**Do we need a dedicated migration specialist?**


Yes, particularly if you’re moving years of historical data.


[Reconciliation Services](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/nonprofit-crm-migration-reconciliation-services/) used a dedicated Giveffect migration specialist to move nearly 15 years of records across five systems, including custom fixes for fields that didn’t map cleanly.


**What should we do with historical data that doesn’t fit the new system’s fields?**


Build a specific structured field for it instead of dumping it into a catch-all “notes” field. Catch-all fields are faster short-term but make future segmentation and automation much harder to do well.
